provider_query: In the Hacker News discussion of SQLite as an application file format, read both the comment that rejects waiting on disk in the interface and the comment about Windows file-system snapshots
answer:
Both comments are in the June 2020 Hacker News thread on [SQLite as an Application File Format (2014)](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23508923) (sqlite.org/appfileformat.html).

**Rejects waiting on disk in the UI**

1. **lillecarl** ([comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23552225)): “If the user interface depends on synchronous IO something is very wrong.”
2. **sdinsn** ([comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23514509)): blocking the UI thread is poor design and cannot be blamed on SQLite.
3. **yellowapple** ([comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23513977)): do not block the UI thread; show a loading indicator while another thread does the transaction. The slow part is the disk, not SQLite.
4. **ori_b** ([comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23510880)), the parent they reply to: a later UI action may still need the previous disk operation to finish.

**Windows file-system snapshots**

5. **int_19h** ([comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23546691)): Windows once had snapshot-based transactions across the whole NTFS filesystem; that feature was deprecated, and the filesystem model has not moved on.
6. **corysama** ([comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23510271)), the parent: atomic file writes are harder than they look; a mid-write shutdown garbles custom formats, which is why the author used SQLite or LMDB (and points at danluu.com/file-consistency/).
7. **hedora** ([comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23510704)): POSIX (and, the author believes, Windows) can durably replace a file with temp write, fsync, close, rename, and sync; skipping the syncs loses data on some systems.
8. **SonOfLilit** ([comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23511635)): journals keep the filesystem consistent, not arbitrary application files; SQLite’s own journaling and careful flush is what gives durability without rewriting the whole document.

(I am the author) Some of the use-cases of mojo I could think of:
1\. Rollbacking DDL changes (like create table, adding columns, etc)
2\. (My use-case) Multiple readers-single writer. Readers read old versions. Writers do not block readers and vice-versa. Note: this is different than reading+writing in the same version can still happen but with database-level locking.
3\. Extension of #2: The older versions read from S3 so that lamda can read.
4\. Extension of #3: Readers reading from old immutable snapshots makes the database as a queue of complex changes with indexes and all the benefits of SQL.
5\. Backups and replication.
Oh: I have change the license to MIT | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | ![](https://news.ycombinator.com/s.gif) | | [quietbritishjim](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=quietbritishjim) [on Aug 29, 2022](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32633452) \| [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32629548) \| [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32629171)\[–\]
For no. 2, WAL mode has this property, why not just use that? Is it for finer control over which version the readers see? | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | ![](https://news.ycombinator.com/s.gif) | | [devnull3](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=devnull3) [on Aug 29, 2022](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32634691) \| [root](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32629548) \| [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32633452) \| [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32629171)\[–\]

This seems great, also in performance, but why would you use this over making plain file copy-based backups, since SQLite is single file based? I'd assume this solution might be preferable because it saves deltas instead of absolute, but the Readme does not say so. If the main advantage here is on-the-fly selecting from different versions, granted, that is unique, even though I cannot really imagine a production use case for this.
So far, I have been using file copies and GFS backup scheme based solutions like Borg, which also does deltas in chunks, compression, and encryption. Perhaps with Borg one should better even backup SQL dumps instead of db files, I don't know. | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | ![](https://news.ycombinator.com/s.gif) | | [devnull3](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=devnull3) [on Aug 28, 2022](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32629320) \| [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32629171) \| [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32630892)\[–\]
Only modified pages go into a version data file \[1\]

don't you get the same benefit if you version controlled the db file with git? with git, each commit saves a diff from the previous one as a blob. the difference is that in git, in addition to the diffs, you also have to create a working copy of the db, which means you use up at least 2x the storage your system uses. in your implementation, the diff blobs _are_ the live db, which saves you ~2x storage. is that the main benefit? | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | ![](https://news.ycombinator.com/s.gif) | | [devnull3](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=devnull3) [on Aug 29, 2022](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32634304) \| [root](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32629171) \| [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32631981) \| [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32628367#32630339)\[–\]

hm but can't you do the same thing (gzipping) with the db itself?

⭐ Community Toolkit SQLite logo

SQLite is a lightweight, serverless, self-contained SQL database engine. It stores the entire database as a single file on disk — no separate server process to run or configure. The Aspire SQLite integration (from the Aspire Community Toolkit) lets you model a SQLite database as a first-class resource in your AppHost, then hand the file-path connection information to any consuming app — regardless of language.

## Why use SQLite with Aspire

Section titled “Why use SQLite with Aspire”

Adding SQLite through Aspire — rather than hardcoding file paths and connection strings — gives you: [...] Ideal for local development, unit tests, and desktop apps. No container to spin up, no server to configure — SQLite runs in-process directly from a single file on disk.
 Consistent connection info across languages. Once you reference the SQLite resource from a consuming app, Aspire injects the database file path as an environment variable in a predictable format that works from C#, TypeScript, Python, Go, or any other language.
 Optional browser-based UI. The `WithSqliteWeb` method adds a lightweight `sqlite-web` container alongside your database so you can inspect and query it during development. [...] The hosting integration lives in your AppHost project and models the SQLite database file as a resource. Because SQLite is an embedded, file-based database, there is no container to start — Aspire simply tracks the database file path and injects it into consuming apps as environment variables.

Getting there is a two-step process: model the SQLite resource in your AppHost, then connect to the database from each app that needs it.
